Consult Summary:
- 32-year-old female nurse with 7 days of fever, night sweats, myalgia, nausea, and fatigue after recent travel to Vietnam; being referred for clinical examination and blood testing including malaria films.

History:
- Presenting complaint:
  - Fever for approximately 7 days with intermittent sensations of being very hot and very cold.
  - Profuse sweating, including night sweats.
  - Generalized muscle aches.
  - Nausea with reduced oral intake and decreased drinking.
  - Marked fatigue and malaise.
- Timeline/progression:
  - Symptoms began about one week (7 days) prior to this consult.
  - No clear improvement despite symptomatic OTC medications; ibuprofen and paracetamol "take the edge off" only.
- Exacerbating/relieving factors:
  - Patient reports taking over-the-counter paracetamol and ibuprofen at recommended doses daily; slight symptomatic improvement only.
- Associated symptoms / review of systems:
  - No cough, no cold symptoms, no sore throat.
  - No ear pain.
  - No diarrhea.
  - No neck stiffness.
  - Headache at baseline only (chronic, screen/weather related), no new severe headache or migraine currently.
  - No rash.
  - No joint swelling or new joint pain (chronic back pain only).
  - No urinary symptoms (no dysuria, no frequency).
- Travel/exposure history:
  - Returned from Vietnam 4 weeks ago.
  - Travel included rural areas, trekking, cycling, exposure to farmland; trip described as "quite adventurous."
  - Reports having taken malaria prophylaxis but cannot recall the drug name; patient believes it was a daily regimen and stated she "took another one on top of the first one" (prophylaxis details not documented / patient uncertain).
- Functional impact:
  - Working as a nurse; currently struggling at work due to fatigue; advised not to return to work until evaluated.

Past Medical History:
- Chronic back pain attributed to prolonged sitting/poor posture; currently under physiotherapy (exercises for posture and back strengthening).
- No other major past medical illnesses reported.

Medications:
- Seroxat (dose/route/frequency not documented).
- Paracetamol — over-the-counter, taken at recommended dose daily for current illness (dose/route/frequency not fully documented).
- Ibuprofen — over-the-counter, taken at recommended dose daily for current illness (dose/route/frequency not fully documented).

Allergies:
- Pollen (hay fever).
- No drug allergies reported.

Social History:
- Occupation: Nurse.
- Employment: Currently working but finding it difficult due to illness; advised to avoid work until assessed.
- Smoking: Denies tobacco use.
- Alcohol: Describes moderate alcohol intake.
- Exercise: Moderate physical exercise a few times per week.
- Vaccinations: Reports up to date with occupational vaccinations (Hepatitis B and similar).

Family History:
- Father died of a myocardial infarction at approximately age 68.
- No other family history details provided.

Physical Examination:
- No vital signs documented.
- No physical examination findings documented in the transcript.

Investigations:
- Planned/requested:
  - Thick and thin blood films for malaria.
  - Blood tests including inflammatory markers (specific tests not all enumerated in transcript).
- No investigation results available at time of consult.

Assessment & Plan:
- Issue 1: Acute febrile illness with systemic symptoms (7 days)
  - Assessment: Unexplained fever with night sweats, myalgia, nausea, and fatigue; no clear localizing symptoms identified on history.
  - Plan:
    - Arrange in-person clinical examination in clinic (central London) or advise attendance to local A&E if more convenient/urgent.
    - Perform targeted blood tests after clinical review.
    - Patient advised not to work until assessment and investigations are complete.
    - Administrative team to contact patient to arrange same-day clinic appointment; patient to call number in consultation note to confirm booking.
- Issue 2: Travel-associated infection risk (recent travel to Vietnam)
  - Assessment: Recent rural travel with exposures raises concern for malaria and other travel-related infections; patient reports taking malaria prophylaxis but details uncertain.
  - Plan:
    - Request thick and thin blood films specifically to evaluate for malaria.
    - Request inflammatory markers and other blood tests as directed by examining clinician.
    - Urgency of testing to be determined by findings on physical examination.
- Issue 3: Symptomatic management and safety
  - Assessment: Patient has partial symptomatic relief from OTC antipyretics but remains unwell.
  - Plan:
    - Continue supportive measures as appropriate until further evaluation (patient currently taking paracetamol and ibuprofen at recommended doses).
    - Clinician to document requested tests and reasoning in notes to facilitate urgent assessment if patient attends other services (e.g., A&E).
    - Follow-up arranged after clinic assessment and test results (specific follow-up timeframe not documented).

General Plan items:
- Administrative booking to be arranged; patient to attend clinic same day if possible.
- If patient cannot attend clinic, patient may present to local A&E with clinician's note requesting malaria films and blood tests.

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - Vital signs (temperature, heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation) not documented.
  - Physical examination findings absent.
  - Exact medication doses, routes, and frequencies for Seroxat, paracetamol, and ibuprofen not documented.
  - Exact name and regimen of malaria prophylaxis not documented.
  - Specific blood test panel (beyond malaria films and "inflammatory markers") not fully enumerated.
  - No laboratory or imaging results available.
- Internal conflicts from transcript:
  - Patient cannot recall the name of malaria prophylaxis; she states it was "daily" and also states she "took another one on top of the first one" — regimen and exact agents uncertain.
  - No other direct contradictions identified.
- Transcript quality:
  - Overall clear and audible; occasional hesitations and minor repetitions but sufficient for clinical documentation.
